Most importantly, the stock trades at a negative price-to-book multiple of -0.61x based on a share price of ₹ 8.05 against a book value of ₹ -13.3 [E1]. Furthermore, momentum is clearly breaking upward as the equity sits entirely at the top, or 100% of the way up, of its 52-week range between a low of 6 and a high of 8 [E4]. Conceded: [E8]. TMT (I) Ltd trades at a microscopic market capitalisation of ₹ 3.99 Cr [E2] while carrying a deeply negative book value of ₹ -13.3, resulting in a meaningless price-to-book ratio of -0.61x [E1]. This negative equity base points directly to a balance sheet that has been eroded by sustained operational failure rather than prudent asset write-downs. The underlying business engine is actively destroying capital, evidenced by a dismal ROCE of -22.2% [E5]. Top-line metrics confirm terminal decay, with compounded sales growth at 0% over 10 years [E6] and actively contracting by -20% over 5 years [E7]. Compounding these fundamental weaknesses, the company returns nothing to its investors, offering a dividend yield of 0.00% [E3]. Despite this catastrophic operational reality, the stock sits at the absolute peak of its 52-week range at ₹ 8.05 [E1, E4], reflecting a speculative disconnection from reality that completely ignores the severe insolvency risk embedded in the filings.

Conceded: the market cap is indeed a microscopic ₹ 3.99 Cr [E2]. However, calling a negative price-to-book ratio of -0.61x an asset bargain ignores the reality that a book value of ₹ -13.3 [E1] indicates severe structural insolvency rather than undervalued worth. While the bull points to momentum at the top of its 52-week range [E4], trading at the high of a stagnant range offers little fundamental comfort when 10-year sales growth is entirely dead at 0% [E6] and 5-year sales have contracted by 20% [E7]. The cited 10-year profit growth of 6% [E8] is entirely hollow given that the return on capital employed sits deep in negative territory at -22.2% [E5], confirming the business destroys capital rather than compounding it. Finally, the complete lack of a safety net is underscored by a dividend yield of 0.00% [E3], leaving outside shareholders exposed to total value erosion without any cash return.
